title: Artificial Intelligence and the Judiciary — Sir Geoffrey Vos MR, lecture to the Judicial Institute for Scotland (Edinburgh, 30 April 2026)
pub: Judiciary of England and Wales (judiciary.uk) — Judicial Institute for Scotland, Parliament Square, Edinburgh
author: Sir Geoffrey Vos

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Vos accepts selective, human-bounded deployment and materially extends the cluster into judicial-system design: routine adjudication may become machine-directed, while rights-sensitive decisions remain human and deployment requires transparent digital infrastructure, public debate, consent, legislation and oversight. His stronger substitution forecast is predictive rather than evidence of general competence.
qs: First, in a number of lectures, I have suggested that, in the world of ever-more capable AI, society in general and the legal community in particular needs urgently to work out what judicial decisions can or should be appropriately informed or taken by AI and what judicial decisions ought never to be taken by AI.

We need to create transparent online Digital Justice Systems that deliver solutions quickly effectively and at proportionate cost, making full and appropriate use of AI and other developing technologies.

st.t: Court responsibility: AI requires lifecycle supervision
st.an: Vos supports supervised judicial AI and continued human responsibility, especially for final appeals and legal development. Although he predicts wider machine involvement in routine adjudication, he conditions replacement of human decisions on informed consent, legislative safeguards and careful democratic debate.
qs: In a democratic society, citizens and businesses should, I have said, only be required to give up the right to have their obligations determined by a human judicial decision in favour of machine-made judicial decisions with their eyes open, with their fully informed consent and after the necessary legislative changes have been made following a mature and careful debate.
First, following on from what I have just said, human judges will surely still be needed to make the final appellate decisions about a human's basic legal rights.

st.t: Machine judging: Accuracy cannot establish legitimate authority
st.an: Vos accepts that machine reliability and economic efficiency do not by themselves confer legitimate judicial authority. Although he predicts machine determination of routine cases, he conditions imposed adjudication on informed consent, legislative change and democratic debate, while preserving human roles in rights appeals, legal development and public confidence.
qs: In a democratic society, citizens and businesses should, I have said, only be required to give up the right to have their obligations determined by a human judicial decision in favour of machine-made judicial decisions with their eyes open, with their fully informed consent and after the necessary legislative changes have been made following a mature and careful debate.
Fourthly, the delivery of justice is as much about the confidence that humans have in the system as it is about the precise outcomes.

kp.k: AI will accelerate legal and judicial work
kp.d: Vos predicts AI use across every aspect of lawyers’ and judges’ work, asserting that change is already underway and will enable faster justice at more proportionate cost. He presents this as his assessment rather than a quantified productivity finding.
qs: It is no secret that I think that AI will be used in every aspect of the work of lawyers and judges.
In my view, the use of AI will speed up legal and judicial work, and will allow justice to be delivered more quickly and at more proportionate cost.

kp.k: Economics will drive automation of routine judicial decisions
kp.d: Vos predicts dedicated programs will decide many routine cases as reliably as human judges. Initially contingent on party agreement, acceptance will, he expects, rapidly become automatic because of speed and cost advantages. He expressly characterises the potential extent of automation as a guess and reports existing AI assistance to judges in China, Brazil and Argentina.
qs: It is now inevitable that basic economics will dictate that routine judicial decision-making will be informed or directed by machines.

They will, in the first instance, be used only with the agreement of the parties, but that acceptance will rapidly become automatic, as the parties to disputes realise that it is far quicker and far cheaper to allow a machine to decide run-of-the-mill legal questions.
But I would guess that it will go further than many may now imagine.
We can already see extensive usage of AI to inform judges taking decisions in China, Brazil and Argentina.

kp.k: Compensation assessments illustrate potential algorithmic adjudication
kp.d: Vos cites the French academics of Le Club des Juristes as recommending consideration of algorithmic systems in compensation litigation. He reports their characterisation of personal injury damages assessment as substantially mechanical or algorithmic, conditional on access to every relevant recent court authority; this is a reported recommendation, not a demonstrated performance result.
qs: "[t]he use of algorithmic systems, including AI, should also be considered in compensation litigation, such as personal injury compensation".

Le Club des Juristes identified that a determination of the personal injury damages to which a claimant is entitled is very much a mechanical or algorithmic exercise once the machine can have access to every relevant recent court authority on such assessments.

kp.k: Replacing human adjudication requires informed consent and legislation
kp.d: Vos urges urgent debate about which decisions AI may inform or take and which it should never take. He distinguishes final judicial decisions from administrative decisions because courts provide the last opportunity to assert rights. He argues that surrendering human adjudication requires fully informed consent, mature debate and legislative change.
qs: society in general and the legal community in particular needs urgently to work out what judicial decisions can or should be appropriately informed or taken by AI and what judicial decisions ought never to be taken by AI.

In a democratic society, citizens and businesses should, I have said, only be required to give up the right to have their obligations determined by a human judicial decision in favour of machine-made judicial decisions with their eyes open, with their fully informed consent and after the necessary legislative changes have been made following a mature and careful debate.

kp.k: Human roles persist through rights, development and explanation
kp.d: Reprising his 17 April 2026 Exeter lecture, Vos identifies enduring human functions: final appellate decisions on basic rights, development of legal principles, helping people understand and accept machine decisions, sustaining confidence, and explaining complexity. He treats explanatory work as crucial to the legal community’s survival, distinguishing rapid machine decisions from slower human understanding and acceptance.
qs: human judges will surely still be needed to make the final appellate decisions about a human's basic legal rights.
humans will remain crucial to the development of legal principles for the benefit of humanity as human culture and human society adapts to the machine age.
Humans will remain instrumental in guiding and assisting other humans towards the understanding and acceptance of machine-made decision-making.
Lawyers will still be needed to explain complexity in a world of ever more capable machines. That will be crucial to the survival of the legal community.

kp.k: Access pressures can conflict with appropriate AI deployment
kp.d: Vos argues that contemporary expectations of equal justice for vulnerable and privileged people create pressure for machine adjudication, particularly in systems handling large caseloads. He warns that those pressures may override consideration of suitability and predicts dissatisfaction unless introduction is careful and consensual, with substantial human advice and supervision.
qs: Now, the citizens and businesses of our countries expect to see a system where justice is available equally to the least privileged and the most vulnerable in our society as it is to the most wealthy and the most privileged.
The pressure to adopt machine-made judicial decisions may not pay adequate regard to the question of whether such decision-making is appropriate for the types of case concerned.
machine-made judicial decisions are also likely to lead to high levels of dissatisfaction unless the processes are very carefully and consensually introduced.
The need for human lawyers and advisers and human supervision is likely to be very significant.

kp.k: Rule-of-law protections must guide judicial automation
kp.d: Vos frames the rule of law as protection against state abuse, rather than the imposition of law by legal professionals. He argues that equal, accessible and predictable protection of rights becomes more important as time and economic pressures encourage machine involvement in adjudication; poor public understanding risks inappropriate AI uses escaping scrutiny.
qs: The rule of law is really about the protection of private citizens against the abuse of power by the state.
And those protections will be increasingly important as the pressures of time and economics force us to consider allowing machines to inform or make judicial decisions.
If the importance of justice and the rule of law is not properly understood, there is an enhanced risk that inappropriate uses of AI will pass unnoticed under the radar without proper scrutiny.

kp.k: Existing legal safeguards face interpretation and possible revision
kp.d: Vos describes article 14 of the EU AI Act as requiring human oversight for high-risk justice systems and article 22 GDPR as seemingly preventing automated decisions affecting legal rights. He identifies whether machines can constitute an independent or impartial tribunal under article 6 ECHR as unresolved. He anticipates interpretation over time, possible amendment pressures and new legislation that legal-community debate could help shape.
qs: Obviously, article 14 of the EU's AI Act makes justice systems into high-risk systems that require human oversight.
Likewise, article 22 of the GDPR seemingly prevents automated decisions that affect a data-subject's legal rights.
And then there is the massively difficult question of whether a machine could ever be an "independent or impartial tribunal" within the meaning of article 6 of the ECHR.
The effect of these provisions will be worked out over time, but there may be pressures to amend or change the provisions themselves.

kp.k: AI increasingly mediates initial legal advice and claims
kp.d: Vos asserts near-universal first recourse to publicly available AI for legal advice and widespread AI creation of claim documents. He separately identifies law firms and corporate clients using dedicated products Harvey and Legora. These are broad assertions without usage statistics or a supporting survey in the speech.
qs: We already know that almost everyone's first port of call for legal advice is to ask a publicly available AI such as ChatGPT, CoPilot, Claude or Gemini.
We also know that many legal claim documents are then created by these same programmes.
Law firms and many of their corporate clients are using dedicated legal advice programmes such as Harvey or Legora as their first port of call.

kp.k: Online knowledge changes legal education's perceived value
kp.d: Vos argues that readily available AI and internet information makes lengthy, expensive formal study harder to justify to younger people. He nevertheless distinguishes legal reasoning and process from factual knowledge and notes that legal qualifications remain necessary for practice.
qs: For younger people today, there have to be better reasons to embark on a lengthy, expensive and detailed course of study than just education for the sake of education.
If we are talking about legal studies, there are, of course, such reasons, since an understanding of the legal process and of legal reasoning is not just a question of facts or knowledge.
And legal qualifications remain necessary to enter legal practice.

kp.k: Digital justice should route users toward trusted resolution
kp.d: Vos describes the Digital Justice System being created in England and Wales, underpinned by Part II of the Judicial Review and Courts Act 2022 and the Online Procedure Rules Committee. Its intended function is to direct citizens to trusted information, advice and dispute-resolution services, avoiding lengthy and expensive proceedings where possible. It must accommodate users who have already consulted search engines or AI.
qs: That Digital Justice System is underpinned by Part II of the Judicial Review and Courts Act 2022 and the Online Procedure Rules Committee, which I chair.

The idea is that any citizen with a legal problem can go online and be directed to the trusted legal information or advice and the trusted dispute resolution service that they need to resolve their particular kind of dispute.

But that does not reduce or devalue the importance of a functioning and available online justice system that provides legal advice and information and dispute resolution quickly and cheaply without the need for lengthy and expensive court proceedings, even online ones.

kp.k: Generational expectations favour accessible outcomes over courtroom formality
kp.d: Vos argues that younger generations consume information differently, are not necessarily less capable of understanding complexity, and are more receptive to cheap, effective online resolution and machine decisions. He predicts expectations of predominantly online outcomes, reserving court attendance for grave and important circumstances, and urges designers not to assume younger people will adopt older generations’ habits.
qs: whilst it is quite wrong to assume that younger generations are less able to discern truth from falsehood or to grasp complex concepts, they do not come to their understandings and principles in the same way as the older generations did, and mostly still do.
In terms of legal dispute, they see no point in the formality of time-consuming legal proceedings if matters can be resolved cheaply and effectively online.
They will require those outcomes to be delivered in most cases online without needless attendances in court save in the most grave and important circumstances.

kp.k: Service redesign communicates legitimacy better than judicial publicity
kp.d: Vos recommends engaging younger generations in rebuilding justice systems and using AI and social media as opportunities for participation. He argues that actual delivery of effective digital justice will communicate the rule of law’s relevance better than judicial videos. Emphasising everyday civil need, he estimates that some 15 million people in England and Wales encounter a civil dispute annually, including minor consumer disputes.
qs: In England and Wales, I estimate that some 15 million people encounter some kind of civil dispute every year, even if that civil dispute is only a dispute with a utility company or an argument about a purchase on eBay.
AI and social media themselves provide good opportunities to engage younger generations in the development of an appropriate justice system for the new machine age.
Actual delivery of technologically enhanced judicial solutions will be far more effective than any amount of judicial Tik-Tok videos seeking to explain the value of the rule of law.
we need to engage them in the process of rebuilding those systems so as to be fit to serve them.

kp.k: Vos rejects technological scepticism and professional immunity
kp.d: Vos asserts that early claims AI would never be useful or overcome hallucinated case names and facts have largely been falsified, without presenting measured error rates. He challenges beliefs that judges’ work will remain substantially unaffected, while maintaining that justice is distinctive and human judicial decision-making will remain necessary.
qs: AI would never be useful or, more commonly, it would never overcome its tendency to hallucinate case names or facts.

In fact, these things have already largely been falsified and everyone now knows that AI will indeed be valuable, useful, indeed invaluable, in almost every single human endeavour and professional activity.
Many want to believe that justice is so special and that lawyers and judges are indispensable and immune from the ravages of the AI revolution.
Nonetheless, the lawyers and judges of today must embrace technology to deliver justice in a more streamlined way.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Vos predicts pervasive AI use, cheaper and faster legal work, and economically driven automation of routine judicial decisions, while maintaining significant roles for human judges, lawyers and advisers.
pts.d: In paragraphs 2–4, Sir Geoffrey Vos says AI adoption is already changing legal and judicial work and predicts its use in every aspect of that work, accelerating justice and making costs more proportionate. In paragraphs 9–13, he predicts that economic pressures will make machine-informed or machine-directed routine adjudication inevitable; dedicated programs will decide many routine cases as reliably as judges, and parties' agreement will rapidly become commonplace because of speed and cost advantages. He cites personal injury damages assessment as a possible application, drawing on a French report rather than presenting an independently established finding. He explicitly labels the eventual extent of automated adjudication a guess. In paragraphs 14–15 and 22, he predicts continuing human roles in final appellate decisions on basic rights, developing legal principles, explaining complexity, helping people understand and accept machine decisions, and maintaining confidence through advice and supervision. He also predicts substantial dissatisfaction if machine adjudication is not introduced carefully and consensually. In paragraph 25, he asserts that publicly available AI is already the first source of legal advice for almost everyone, that it generates many claim documents, and that law firms and many corporate clients first consult dedicated products such as Harvey and Legora. In paragraphs 21, 30–32 and 39–48, he argues that universal-access expectations and caseload pressures will encourage automation, and that younger users will expect predominantly online, quick and affordable justice. He presents England and Wales' developing Digital Justice System as a route to trusted information, advice and dispute resolution without lengthy court proceedings, with AI providing significant assistance rather than being synonymous with the entire digital system. In paragraph 43, he asserts that initial scepticism about AI's usefulness and hallucinations has largely been falsified and that AI will be invaluable across professional activities, including law.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The speech relies principally on Vos's institutional perspective, economic reasoning and asserted observations, supplemented by a French academic report, international examples and an existing digital-justice framework; it supplies no measured AI performance or adoption results.
pts.d: For routine adjudication, Vos reasons from speed and cost incentives and cites Le Club des Juristes' report, Intelligence Artificielle et justice civile: perspectives and ambitions. He reports its recommendation to consider algorithmic systems in compensation litigation and its characterization of personal injury damages assessment as mechanical or algorithmic when relevant recent authorities are available. This is supporting authority, not a demonstrated implementation or accuracy study. He also points to extensive AI use informing judges in China, Brazil and Argentina, without naming systems, quantifying usage or reporting outcomes. His predictions about enduring human roles draw on arguments from his own earlier lectures concerning rights, legal development, comprehension, acceptance and public confidence. The sweeping claims about AI-first legal advice, claim-document generation, generational attitudes and the overcoming of earlier scepticism are not accompanied by surveys, benchmarks or measured hallucination rates. His account of the Digital Justice System identifies Part II of the Judicial Review and Courts Act 2022 and the Online Procedure Rules Committee, which he chairs, as its institutional foundation, but supplies no evaluated cost, speed or access outcomes. His estimate that around 15 million people in England and Wales encounter a civil dispute each year provides context for demand rather than evidence of an AI effect; no method is supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Vos describes adoption as already underway in April 2026 and urges rapid reform, but gives no fixed automation timetable; legitimate substitution for human adjudication is conditioned on informed consent, debate and legislative change.
pts.d: The lecture is dated 30 April 2026. Present-tense claims concern AI-assisted legal advice, document creation, international judicial use and the emerging Digital Justice System. Future predictions use terms such as 'rapidly' and 'inevitable' without specifying dates or adoption percentages. Vos distinguishes AI informing a human judge from a machine taking the decision itself. He expects routine machine adjudication initially to require parties' agreement and predicts acceptance will rapidly become automatic; separately, he insists that surrendering the right to human adjudication should require fully informed consent and legislative changes after mature debate. The damages-assessment example is conditional on access to every relevant recent authority. He leaves the outer limits of automated adjudication unresolved and calls for decisions about which judicial functions should never be automated. He expects human judges to remain necessary for final appellate determinations of basic rights. Careful, consensual introduction, human advice and supervision are conditions for acceptance and confidence. He identifies potential constraints in EU AI Act article 14, GDPR article 22 and ECHR article 6, presenting their effects as matters to be worked out and anticipating possible new domestic and federal legislation. His digital-justice vision also depends on appropriate AI use and engaging the generations the system will serve.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted changes affect judges, practising lawyers, corporate legal buyers, unrepresented litigants and the broader public, especially users seeking affordable civil justice and younger generations expecting online resolution.
pts.d: Judges face both assistance and potential substitution in routine adjudication, while retaining roles in fundamental-rights appeals, legal development and public confidence. Lawyers and advisers face changes to initial advice and document preparation but retain substantial explanatory, advisory and supervisory work; Vos does not quantify job losses, staffing changes or fee effects. Law firms and corporate clients are identified as current users of dedicated legal-AI products; Harvey and Legora appear as software products, not providers delivering legal work in place of firms. Litigants in person and other advice seekers are described as already consulting general-purpose AI and using it to prepare claims. Parties to routine disputes may gain quicker, cheaper decisions but face questions about consent, human adjudication and acceptance. Personal injury claimants are a specifically identified potential application group for algorithmic damages assessment. Citizens and small businesses with civil, family or administrative problems are intended beneficiaries of trusted online advice and resolution; the ambition includes the least privileged and most vulnerable rather than only enterprise cost savings. High-caseload justice systems face particularly acute pressure to automate, potentially without adequate attention to suitability. Younger generations are presented as expecting efficient online outcomes and as necessary participants in system design. Vos's institutional proposal centres on England and Wales, while his arguments address lawyers and judges across Europe and beyond.
